Article Title: Atovio launches Nino and X wearable air purifiers; price starts at Rs 3,499
Article Text:
Atovio launches Nino and X wearable air purifiers; price starts at Rs 3,499

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Atovio has expanded its product portfolio with the launch of Atovio Nino, India's first wearable air purifier made for kids. Priced at Rs 3,499, Nino is a panda-shaped pendant on a chain for children aged 4 and above, available in pink, blue and black. Nino, Atovioa says, uses ion technology with no filter and no fan. It releases negatively charged ions that attach to airborne particles such as PM2.5 and PM10, as well as bacteria and viruses. The particles clump together and settle out of the child's breathing space. With no fan it runs silently, and with no filter there is nothing to replace. Atovio states that Nino produces no ozone, with a reading below 0.008 ppm at an NABL-accredited lab.Atovio Nino comes with a single button on the panda's nose that switches between Normal mode, Turbo mode and off, while small LED dots on its face show the battery level. Nino charges over USB Type-C and runs for around 72 hours on a full charge, which covers the morning commute, the classroom, study time, indoor play areas and family trips.In laboratory tests at the National Aerosol Facility at IIT Kanpur, Atovio's ion technology cut airborne particle concentration by 90% within 25 minutes in a sealed chamber.A separate test at the Kitasato Research Center in Japan recorded a 99.2% reduction in airborne viruses within 30 minutes with Nino in Turbo mode. In real-world conditions, the technology has also shown close to 44% lower inhalation of pollutants at IIT Kanpur's National Aerosol Facility.Alongside Nino, Atovio also launched Atovio X, India's first smart wearable air purifier, following the launch of the Atovio Pebble last year. Atovio X adds app controls and an Airshift mode that adjusts purification automatically based on how the wearer moves. It is a rounded, disc-shaped pendant with concentric ridges, worn on a metal chain, and comes in five colours: Obsidian Black, Sapphire Frost, Cosmic White, Coral Pink and Carbon Eclipse.It is priced at Rs 4,999, while a personalized edition with a name or initials costs ₹Rs 5,299. Nino and Atovio X are available on Atovio's website and on e-commerce platforms.Commenting on the launch, Anmay Shahlot, Co-Founder, Atovio, said, "Parents have plenty of ways to clean the air at home, but children spend a big part of their day away from it. We wanted to build something kids would be excited to wear and not something they need to be convinced to wear. A friendly character, one button and silent operation make personal clean air easy for a child and reassuring for a parent.As concerns about air quality follow families from home to school and everywhere in between, Atovio plans to keep building wearable products that fit real routines and are designed for the people who use them. Whether it is a commuter, a traveller or a four-year-old with a panda around their neck, the goal stays the same: clean air that goes wherever you go.”
Article Summary: Atovio has expanded its product portfolio with the launch of Atovio Nino, India's first wearable air purifier made for kids. Priced at Rs 3,499, Nino is a panda-shaped pendant on a chain for children aged 4 and above, available in pink, blue and black. Nino uses ion technology with no filter and no fan.

Article Title: California Wendy’s customer is suing the burger chain and the company behind its checkout software, alleging they worked together to raise menu prices across the US
Article Text:
How Wendy’s allegedly used data from its checkout software

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that fast-food chains should be allowed to coordinate menu prices? Yes, it's necessary for consistency. No, each restaurant should set its own prices. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A longtime Wendy’s customer in California is suing the fast-food chain and NCR Voyix, the company behind its checkout software. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the lawsuit alleges that they worked together to raise menu prices across the US. Andy Garcia says Wendy’s used detailed sales data from independently owned restaurants to coordinate prices, leaving customers like him paying more than they would have if the locations had competed on price. He filed the proposed class action 3 in federal court in Maryland.Garcia says he eats at Wendy’s at least once a week. He is asking to represent people who bought one or more menu items at any US Wendy’s from January 1, 2022, whether the restaurant was run by a franchisee or by Wendy’s itself. The suit seeks monetary damages and a court order to stop the alleged pricing coordination.At the centre of the lawsuit is Aloha, the point-of-sale system supplied by NCR Voyix. The complaint says Wendy’s required franchisees to use the software and provide detailed sales and pricing information, the Reuters report noted. That included data from individual transactions. Garcia alleges that Wendy’s pooled and shared that information across its restaurant network and used it to coordinate menu prices.ReutersThe case turns on who actually decided what customers paid. Restaurants can carry the same Wendy’s name while operating under different owners. Garcia argues that those owners should have been able to compete for customers by setting their own prices. The complaint alleges that Wendy’s instead became a “common decision-maker” for thousands of locations. In Garcia’s account, that arrangement removed an incentive for individual operators to charge less.Allen Neumark, one of Garcia’s lawyers, said Wendy’s tells investors its franchisees set their own prices. He disputed that account, saying centralised pricing came at customers’ expense. Wendy’s and NCR Voyix did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.Wendy’s previously drew scrutiny when it discussed testing dynamic pricing, which can change prices in response to conditions such as demand. Garcia’s complaint focuses on how prices were set across restaurants and the role their sales data allegedly played in those decisions.The case follows a separate lawsuit filed against McDonald’s in October over its use of technology to guide menu prices at US franchises. McDonald’s has denied wrongdoing.
Article Summary: Andy Garcia says Wendy’s used detailed sales data from independently owned restaurants to coordinate prices, leaving customers like him paying more than they would have if the locations had competed on price. Garcia is asking to represent people who bought one or more menu items at any US Wendy's from January 1, 2022, whether the restaurant was run by a franchisee or by Wendy's itself.

Article Title: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani blasts Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang; reminds him how his 'romantic affairs' may hurt Americans; says: Working people in the US didn't sign up for their pensions being tied to
Article Text:
The $81 billion remark made by Zohran Mamdani

Concerns over wealth concentration

AI stocks and market dependence

Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The investigation into Jensen Huang will still run its course

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has criticised the outsized influence of major technology companies on financial markets, using the recent controversy involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as an example of how the personal affairs of powerful executives can affect ordinary Americans. According to a report by Politico, speaking to reporters at a recent press conference, Mamdani said that he was concerned that the financial security of working people could be affected by the developments surrounding one of the technology industry’s most influential leaders. He also emphasised that the workers should not have their retirement savings and pension funds exposed to volatility linked to the personal conduct of corporate executives.“I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang's fidelity to his marriage. And yet for many days that had a massive impact,” Mamdani said.Mamdani also noted a rumoured divorce settlement of about $81 billion, which he said would cover a year of universal child care for every 3- and 4-year-old in the United States. There has been no announcement of a divorce between Huang and his wife.The $81 billion figure is a rumor Mamdani cited, not a confirmed number.Mamdani also talked about the reports and rumours regarding the personal life of Jensen Huang and the potential financial implications that had been discussed in public. Referring to a widely reported estimate of a possible divorce settlement, Mamdani noted that the figure being discussed was approximately $81 billion.According to Mamdani, such a large sum highlights the scale of wealth concentrated in the hands of a small number of individuals. He compared the reported figure with the potential cost of funding universal childcare across the United States for three- and four-year-old children for a year.The mayor then invoked a famous quote from former US Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis, saying, “We can have democracy, we can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few. We cannot have both.”The criticism made by Mamdani goes beyond Huang and Nvidia. He also warned about the excessive reliance on stocks related to artificial intelligence with the broader US economy. He further stressed that dominance of AI companies in public markets raises questions about economic resilience and concentration of power.“When you look at our stock market, and you look at how disproportionately dependent it is on artificial intelligence-related stocks, it cannot help but give you a sense of concern about just how much this technology is now dominant,” he said.Jensen Huang is back in charge at Nvidia, less than two weeks after he quit the company he co-founded. The chipmaker's board has voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO and board director, effective immediately. The board said a series of meetings with Huang left it satisfied with his candour and his ability to lead. It added that input from senior levels of the US government gave it confidence his return poses no national security risk. The move is a complete U-turn from last week, when the same board said it had no plans to bring him back.Huang resigned on November 12, ending a 33-year run as CEO. His exit came days after Nvidia said it would investigate reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Those reports linked him to a woman US officials believe was recruited by China's spy agency. CFO Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO.Huang's return does not end the probe. A committee made up only of independent directors, working with independent counsel, is looking into the foreign intelligence reports. The board said the investigation will proceed to its conclusion. Huang has said he fully supports it and will cooperate.Nvidia is also adding new layers of oversight. The board recently set up a National Security and Export Control Committee, again made up only of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. It is bringing in counsel with national security experience, who will hire specialist advisers of their own. The company has also started a search for a new Chief Compliance Officer, who will report to the board's Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations. Huang and general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to answer questions from US House committees behind closed doors on December 1 and 2.
Article Summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has criticised the outsized influence of major technology companies on financial markets. He used the recent controversy involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as an example of how the personal affairs of powerful executives can affect ordinary Americans. He also stressed that dominance of AI companies in public markets raises questions about economic resilience and concentration of power.

Article Title: Donald Trump wants US companies to build data centres at home, Microsoft’s Brad Smith points to…
Article Text:
What Brad Smith said about US taxing companies that have data center overseas

“Well, my sense is that the president is making an important point, but there's some critical nuance we need to think about as well. The point is sort of analogous to the chip industry. I think the administration might want to see the most advanced frontier models trained in the United States, and- and there's room to have that kind of conversation. The nuance is that there's lots of different kinds of data centers. Most data centers actually don't have AI. They're

cloud services

to stream a video, play a video game, run your business, and those have to be located close to customers. They often now have AI because the business applications, even your video games, have an AI element, and the president talked about say, data centers in Finland. You can't support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey. Those have to be located locally.”

What Donald Trump said about data centres overseas

US President Donald Trump wants American companies to build data centres at home. He has also threatened a tax on those that set them up overseas. Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith pointed to Finland to explain why some facilities need to stay close to customers.Speaking on a recent episode of CBS News’ Face the Nation, Smith said there was room to discuss training the most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models in the US. He said data centres that support services such as video streaming, gaming and business software need to be located near the people and companies that use them.During the CBS interview, Smith said,Speaking at a White House press conference last week, Trump said he wanted US companies to build data centres in the country and threatened penalties for those that build them abroad. He cited concerns about China and drew a parallel with the chip industry, where his administration has pushed for more manufacturing in the US. However, Trump gave no tax rate or timeline during the briefing.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared on the programme before Smith, said he had yet to speak to Trump about the remarks. Bessent said he understood the president’s concern as sensitive technology moving overseas.He said Trump wanted to avoid the kind of dependence on overseas production that had developed in the semiconductor industry.For Microsoft, the scope of any tax would matter. The company has more than 600 data centres across 34 countries. A measure focused on where companies train advanced AI models would affect a narrower set of facilities than a tax covering every new overseas cloud site. As Smith pointed out, a cloud service can also include AI features, so the details would matter for facilities that serve both purposes.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump wants American companies to build data centres at home. He has also threatened a tax on those that set them up overseas. Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith pointed to Finland to explain why some facilities need to stay close to customers.

Article Title: North Korea’s answer to ChatGPT has one request for users: Don’t ask about…
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

North Korea’s new chatbot can field questions about game design and headaches. Politics is off limits.The tool, called Fountain of Wisdom, appears to be the country’s first domestically developed AI chatbot, according to 38 North, a US-based research programme that monitors North Korea. It was shown at an IT exhibition in Pyongyang last month and later appeared in a broadcast on the state television channel Ryongnamsan.Martyn Williams, a senior fellow at the Stimson Centre, which runs 38 North, identified Kim Il-sung University’s AI research institute and Pyongyang software developer Phurunhanul Trading as the organisations behind the chatbot.The interface resembles OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The system can answer science and technology questions in Korean or English and translate text, according to the report. Chat histories visible in the broadcast showed someone asking about game-design software. Another query asked what medicine to take for a headache. The footage offered a glimpse of the kinds of everyday questions the chatbot was built to handle.An on-screen notice made the limits clear. “Do not ask questions with sociopolitical content or uncultured questions,” it said, according to Williams’ translation. The notice also told users they would be responsible for any malicious use of the system.The broadcast offered few clues about what powers Fountain of Wisdom. The developers disclosed neither the model nor the hardware it runs on. Williams suggested the team might have used a foreign open-weight model, whose underlying parameters are available for others to download and adapt. The footage did not establish whether that was the case.Williams noted that North Korean hackers and IT workers already appeared to be using foreign AI tools. In August last year, Anthropic said North Korean operatives had used its Claude chatbot to create false professional identities, pass coding tests and complete technical assignments after landing remote jobs at Fortune 500 technology companies.Anthropic said Claude helped some operatives with limited coding skills or English proficiency secure and keep those jobs. The company banned the accounts it linked to the activity and shared its findings with authorities. The 38 North report did not link Fountain of Wisdom to the employment scheme.
Article Summary: The tool, called Fountain of Wisdom, appears to be the country’s first domestically developed AI chatbot. It was shown at an IT exhibition in Pyongyang last month and later appeared in a broadcast on the state television channel Ryongnamsan.

Article Title: Huawei’s Android alternative hits 100 million installs and overtakes iOS in China
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Huawei’s Android-free operating system has crossed 100 million installations. The milestone gives the Chinese tech giant a foothold in mobile software as it looks to take HarmonyOS beyond its home market.Huawei said the figure covers smartphones, tablets and PCs running HarmonyOS 5, 6 and 7. The company says its ecosystem now offers more than 460,000 apps and services and has over 12 million registered developers, according to a report by South China Morning Post.The strongest gains have come in China. HarmonyOS accounted for 24% of the country’s smartphone operating system market in the second quarter, according to Counterpoint Research. That put Huawei ahead of Apple’s iOS, which had an 18% share, and behind Google’s Android, which led with 58%.The global picture is different. HarmonyOS had a 5% share in the same quarter, while Android accounted for 75% and iOS for 20%. Limited app compatibility remains a hurdle for Huawei overseas, where buyers switching to a HarmonyOS phone may find some of their usual apps unavailable.Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s consumer business group, called the installation milestone a “landmark moment” in a post on Weibo.In September, he told reporters that Huawei would roll out HarmonyOS internationally in stages over the next one to three years.Huawei first launched HarmonyOS in China in August 2019, months after Washington put the company on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US-origin technology. Early versions could run Android apps. That changed with HarmonyOS 5, also known as HarmonyOS Next, which Huawei introduced in 2024 as a fully self-developed operating system.The shift has coincided with Huawei’s smartphone comeback, helped by the use of its own chips. That recovery has given the company more devices on which to put its software. It has also given developers in China a larger market for apps built specifically for HarmonyOS.The overseas push will test whether Huawei can repeat that cycle in markets where Android and iOS already reach almost every smartphone buyer. A wider selection of local banking, payments and transport apps could give shoppers a reason to switch. Developers, in turn, will need to see enough demand to justify building and maintaining those apps.
Article Summary: HarmonyOS now offers more than 460,000 apps and services and has over 12 million registered developers. The strongest gains have come in China. Limited app compatibility remains a hurdle for Huawei overseas, where buyers switching to a HarmonyOS phone may find their usual apps unavailable.

Article Title: Australia passes law that may result in massive fines for Google, Meta and other internet platforms if…
Article Text:
Australia’s another ‘regulatory blow’ to US-based tech giants

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Free speech, privacy and over-censorship concerns

Australia has passed a sweeping new online safety law requiring major internet platforms, including Google and Meta, to proactively eliminate harmful content and features, or risk penalties of up to 5% of their global revenue. The legislation, known as the Digital Duty of Care, will take effect in one year. Replacing an existing patchwork of separate online codes of conduct with a single, all-encompassing law, the rules shift the responsibility directly onto tech companies to prioritise the safety of Australian users. Under the new law, platforms that breach the rules face fines of up to 5% of their global turnover or A$109 million ($72 million), whichever is greater – a steep financial threat for tech giants that generate hundreds of billions of dollars in annual revenue, news agency Reuters reported.“The Digital Duty of Care is a landmark safety reform in the vein of compulsory seatbelts, plain packaging for cigarettes and gun reform. Big Tech can no longer be under any illusions – they are responsible for keeping Australians safe on their platforms, and we will hold them to account if they fail to do so,” Communications Minister Anika Wells said in a statement following the law's passage.The Digital Duty of Care adds to a string of moves by Australia against the largely US-based internet industry, which the government has accused of undermining its right to regulate digital products used within its borders.In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to ban children under 16 from using social media. Moreover, the Australian government also plans to force major internet platforms to pay licensing fees for news content to reimburse news media organisations.While technology companies have broadly supported the government's goal of protecting children and curbing online harm, most opposed the legislation, arguing that it gives government officials too much discretion to decide what qualifies as harmful content. As per the report, industry groups have also cautioned that the threat of severe fines could push platforms to become overly heavy-handed with takedowns simply to avoid punishment.Specifically, the law prohibits material that “encourages or promotes hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality” as well as content that “glorifies crime or encourages dangerous stunts or seriously harmful practices” – broad classifications that free speech advocates warn are open to wide interpretation, the report noted.
Article Summary: Australia has passed a sweeping new online safety law requiring major internet platforms to proactively eliminate harmful content. The legislation, known as the Digital Duty of Care, will take effect in one year. Under the new law, platforms that breach the rules face fines of up to 5% of their global turnover or A$109 million ($72 million), whichever is greater.

Article Title: US Army to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa: What's inside, why officials say it can't wait, how far the dust may travel and safety advice
Article Text:
Iowa Army Ammunition Plant detonation set for 9am CST Wednesday (Picture: Reuters)

Decades-old lead azide has become too unstable to move or open

Army says waiting out the winter is the bigger risk

Water walls, foam and gel blocks will try to trap the lead dust

Lead dust plume could travel up to 100 miles into Missouri

Lead exposure safety tips: stay indoors, recirculate air, wet-clean later

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The US Army will blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, at around 9am CST on Wednesday (8.30pm IST). The stockpile, about 9,700 pounds (roughly 4,400 kg) packed into 68 drums, has crystallised to the point where officials say it could go off on its own as temperatures drop. A federal appeals court cleared the controlled detonation on Monday, though the exact time still depends on the weather.The Army's latest maps show lead dust drifting southwest, with airborne particles possibly reaching 100 miles (about 160 km) into Missouri. FEMA is helping residents of Middletown, a town of about 360 people that borders the plant, relocate before the blast."Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.Lead azide is a primary explosive, the small, sensitive charge used to set off larger munitions such as grenades. The US began using it almost a century ago and moved away from it about 15 years ago because it is so hard to store and transport. In 2009, the country's remaining stock was consolidated at the Iowa facility. Some of it was already more than 60 years old.The compound sat in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums, topped up with a water and ethanol mix so it would not freeze.A routine inspection on March 11 found significant crystallisation on the outside of the barrels. In that state, lead azide is so sensitive to friction that even unscrewing a bolt could trigger a chain reaction. Opening the lids to add more liquid was off the table.Experts from the Army, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and other agencies weighed chemical neutralisation, thermal treatment, relocation and continued storage, and rejected all four. Neutralisation meant opening the drums, while burning or moving the material would expose it to vibration and impact. Leaving it alone was no safer, as cold weather only makes it more volatile."It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when," Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said on Tuesday.The detonation was first set for last Friday, and the date has shifted three times since. The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club went to court to halt it pending an environmental study, and President Donald Trump said the Army would hold off until the court ruled.The drums sit in 80-year-old earth-covered magazines, concrete bunkers that are already cracked and likely to break open. Around them, the Army has stacked sand barriers roughly two storeys high, a water wall built from four 16,000-gallon tanks, gel blocks and two feet of aqueous foam. Misters will soak the surrounding soil, and drones will track lead levels in the air.The last comparable disposal was in Colorado in 1977, when 7,000 pounds of lead azide was detonated in the open with zero mitigation. Even then, 75% of the lead stayed on site, according to Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordnance Disposal Group. The Army expects its new barriers to sharply cut the 25% that escaped back then."We don't believe that the public should be in a panic," said Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle.Earlier projections had the plume heading north, but maps released on Tuesday now point southwest. Heavier particles are expected to settle in a narrow strip 35 to 40 miles (56 to 64 km) long, covering parts of southeastern Iowa and just crossing the Missouri state line.The evacuation zone is a five-mile cone southwest of the plant, plus a one-mile buffer. Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties, and Missouri has activated its State Emergency Operations Center. The US Department of Agriculture estimates 350 farms could be affected.There is no safe level of lead exposure. Infants and children under six, pregnant women and people with heart disease, kidney disease or dementia are the most vulnerable, and officials have urged them to leave the area. FEMA is offering transport, meals and hotel stays through Friday, November 27, via its helpline at 1-800-621-3362.People outside the zone are advised to shut windows and doors, set heating to recirculate and switch off bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans. A fresh furnace filter rated MERV 11 or higher helps, as does a HEPA air purifier. Iowa's health department recommends staying indoors for 24 to 48 hours after the blast.Once officials give the all-clear, surfaces children touch, from play equipment to patios and windowsills, should be wet-cleaned rather than swept dry. Residents worried about property damage can file a claim with the Army on Standard Form 95 within two years.
Article Summary: The US Army will blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. The stockpile, about 9,700 pounds (roughly 4,400 kg) packed into 68 drums, has crystallised to the point where officials say it could go off on its own as temperatures drop. The Army's latest maps show lead dust drifting southwest, with airborne particles possibly reaching 100 miles (about 160 km) into Missouri.

Chinese fast-fashion retailer Shein will pay $100 million to settle claims in the United States that it misled customers about shipping times, product reviews and the origin of cotton used in some of its products. The FTC plans to use the money to reimburse consumers, the official said. The claims relate to complaints from customers who said their orders did not arrive on time, along with allegations that Shein removed negative product reviews and gave misleading information about where cotton used in some products was grown.Founded in China and now headquartered in Singapore, Shein became popular for selling low-priced clothing, including dresses for around $5 and jeans for about $10. This meant customers may not have received a complete picture of other buyers' experiences before making purchases. Another concern involved the origin of cotton used in some Shein products. The company was accused of misrepresenting where the cotton was grown.Shein has also faced scrutiny over allegations that its clothes may contain cotton from China's Xinjiang region. The US government and human rights groups have raised concerns about forced labour involving Uyghur minorities in the region.The US has a law called the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, which bans imports from Xinjiang because of concerns over forced labour.Shein has previously said that it does not use Chinese cotton in products sold in the US. However, questions about the origin of cotton used in its products have continued to attract attention.Shein went public in Hong Kong in September. The latest settlement adds to the challenges facing the fast-fashion retailer as it deals with regulatory scrutiny and questions about its business practices.

Fortnite maker Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney has unexpectedly praised both tech giants, Google and Apple , for never crossing a critical ethical line despite spending six years locked in bitter antitrust courtroom battles and regulatory disputes. In a public “note of appreciation to Apple and Google,” Sweeney credited his longtime legal rivals with steering clear of what he described as a dangerous alliance between government security agencies and major technology firms – a tactic he claimed appears to be behind a smear campaign targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.“This is a note of appreciation to Apple and Google that, through 6 years of harsh antitrust litigation and regulatory advocacy, they never once proposed the sort of corrupt, freedom-ending marriage of state security and big tech that appears to be behind Jensen smear campaign,” Sweeney wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter).While praising Apple and Google for keeping their battles within traditional legal and regulatory bounds, Sweeney aimed sharp criticism at leading artificial intelligence developers Anthropic and OpenAI. Censorship, control, whatever,” Sweeney said.Contrasting that approach with the behaviour of his longtime app store adversaries, Sweeney concluded simply: “Apple and Google did no such thing.”Last year, Sameer Samat, president of the Android Ecosystem at Google, stated on X that Google has “filed a proposed set of changes to Android and Google Play that focus on expanding developer choice and flexibility, lowering fees, and encouraging more competition all while keeping users safe. If approved, this would resolve our litigations.”Sweeney, responded with immediate praise, saying the proposal “genuinely doubles down on Androids original vision as an open platform.”“Google has made an awesome proposal, subject to court approval, to open up Android in the US Epic v Google case and settle our disputes. It genuinely doubles down on Android's original vision as an open platform to streamline competing store installs globally, reduce service fees for developers on Google Play, and enable third-party in-app and web payments,” he added.

Article Title: Sundar Pichai-backed San Francisco-based family foundation recorded $9.2 million in grant payments for the year 2025, filing shows foundation’s largest single payment of $6.16 million not to a directl
Article Text:
Sundar Pichai-backed San Francisco-based family foundation recorded $9.2 million in grant payments for the year 2025

Pichai Family Foundation's donation in 2025

Why Pichai’s family foundation sent $6.16 million to a donor-advised fund

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Pichai Family Foundation, established by Google CEO Sundar Pichai and based in San Francisco, reported nearly $9.2 million in grant payments for the 2025 tax year, according to its latest IRS filing. But its biggest payment did not go to a directly named charity. Around $6.16 million was directed to the GS Donor Advised Philanthropy Fund for Wealth Mgmt in Albany, New York, the filing shows. The payment accounted for nearly two-thirds of the foundation's total grant spending for the year and was listed as general operating support. The filing is available through ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer.The foundation's second-largest payment was around $2 million to the Castilleja School Foundation in Palo Alto. Other recipients included organisations working in education, healthcare, food security and children's welfare. Second Harvest of Silicon Valley received approximately $450,000, while Boys & Girls of the Peninsula was awarded around $125,000. Doctors Without Borders and UNICEF USA each received about $100,000. The foundation also made grants to Peninsula Bridge and Pratham USA, both associated with educational initiatives.Other payments included around $50,000 to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco, $25,000 to the Global Fund for Children and approximately $15,000 to Aarti for Girls. The 2025 filing listed 11 grant payments in total.A donor-advised fund, or DAF, is a charitable giving arrangement that allows donors to contribute money to a fund and recommend grants to eligible organisations over time. The sponsoring organisation retains legal control of the assets and handles the subsequent grantmaking. This means the $6.16 million payment recorded in the Pichai Family Foundation's filing does not identify the final charities that may eventually receive the money. The filing records the transfer to the fund, but does not disclose the fund's subsequent distribution of those assets.The latest figures also point to an increase in the foundation's reported grantmaking. Its 2020 filing recorded seven grants worth approximately $510,000. The available 2022 record showed 11 grants totalling $2.6 million, followed by $4.2 million across 12 grants in 2023 and $6.3 million across 11 grants in 2024.The foundation also made a similar payment of approximately $5.1 million to the same Albany-based donor-advised fund in 2024. Together, the two payments amount to nearly $11.3 million. Across available filings for 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, the foundation reported 52 grants worth approximately $22.9 million, reaching 19 distinct recipients, according to figures compiled by OpenGrants from IRS electronic filing data.
Article Summary: Pichai Family Foundation reported nearly $9.2 million in grant payments for the 2025 tax year. But its biggest payment did not go to a directly named charity. Around $6.16 million was directed to the GS Donor Advised Philanthropy Fund for Wealth Mgmt in Albany, New York.

Article Title: Anthropic's Claude Ship can review, fix and approve code changes without waiting for a human
Article Text:
Claude Ship can approve code changes on its own (Picture: AP)

Claude Approvals lets teams write their own rules for AI sign-offs

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Claude Ship pricing depends on how much code it reviews

Anthropic wants Claude to do more than write code. The company has introduced Claude Ship, a set of AI agents that can review pull requests, fix what breaks and even approve routine code changes on their own, if a team's rules allow it. Now in beta for Claude Team and Enterprise customers with repositories on GitHub, the tool goes after the slowest stretch of software development: the wait between opening a pull request and merging it.Claude Ship brings three pieces together. Code Review, which became generally available in October, reads each pull request against the full codebase and posts verified findings. Two new agents sit on top of it. PR Steward jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts and review comments from Code Review, other tools or teammates. Claude Approvals then decides whether the change is ready to merge.The idea started with Anthropic's own engineers. Claude writes about 90% of Claude Code's code, and the team wanted everything after the pull request "to move that fast too." Between June and September, its merged pull requests more than doubled, while the share later reverted fell by over 40%.Claude Approvals runs on a policy file that teams add to their repository.The rules can be written in natural language and decide which changes Claude can approve alone and which need a person. Anthropic calls it a smarter CODEOWNERS file. Teams can also feed it signals like Code Review findings or their own classifiers.This is a step past Anthropic's earlier position that approving a pull request was still a human call. For now, the company recommends running Approvals in observe-only mode first.PR Steward, meanwhile, is built not to approve or merge anything. After every push, it comments on what it changed and how to undo it. Developers can type @claude to steer it, or @claude stop to make it back off.Developers can try all of this with a new /ship command in Claude Code, which pushes the change, opens the pull request, reviews it and works through feedback and failing checks. In one internal example, a product manager used Claude Tag to fix confusing Analytics API documentation, and the fix merged the same evening.Claude Ship is billed on tokens. Costs depend on the number and size of pull requests, the review level (Quick, Standard or Deep) and how much work PR Steward does. Admins can set spend limits. Claude Approvals has no base charge, though policy classifiers are billed. Running /ship counts as regular Claude Code usage.Eligible Enterprise organisations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits until January 15, 2027.The tool is not available to organisations using Zero Data Retention, the HIPAA configuration or customer-managed encryption keys. The /ship command is rolling out now in Claude Code and the desktop app.
Article Summary: Claude Approvals lets teams write their own rules for AI sign-offs. Code Review reads each pull request against the full codebase and posts verified findings. PR Steward jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts and review comments from Code Review.

Article Title: Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman has advice for tech companies on AI safety: ‘No one relies on …’
Article Text:
AWS CEO compares AI with car safety

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why hype leads to poor risk management

Amazon Web Services (AWS) CEO Matt Garman has a clear message for companies deploying artificial intelligence (AI): stop relying on hope or emergency “kill switches,” and start engineering stronger guardrails around the models. His comments came as fears over rogue AI agents and safety risks continue to ripple across the tech sector. In a 1,300-word blog post, Garman argued that while policymakers and industry leaders debate rules and principles, businesses are already rolling out AI in live production environments. Instead of treating AI safety as an abstract policy issue, he urged companies to apply decades-old software and hardware security discipline right now.“With the right engineering discipline, you can build meaningful, enforceable boundaries around AI systems. You can build containment that operates outside the model’s reach. You can design systems where every meaningful action leaves auditable, tamper-resistant evidence. You can architect controls that don’t depend on the model cooperating with its own constraints,” Garman said.Garman likened AI safety with safety in a car. He said that people do not rely on emergency brakes to be safe, rather there are other components like steering, suspension and so on.“Think about how we approach safety in a car. No one relies on the emergency brake as their main source of protection on the road. The primary brakes, steering, suspension, and navigation are engineered to work together and keep you safe on every drive, and the emergency brake is there as a last resort. AI systems should be engineered the same way, and that work can and should be happening right now, alongside the policy conversations,” he said.In recent months, tech companies have been working on kill switches to terminate rogue AI agents. CrowdStrike introduced AI Kill Switch earlier this month. Design tools company Canva also added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its offerings. Meanwhile, California governor Gavin Newsom also touted an AI kill switch to halt dangerous agents.According to Garman, extreme fear and hype around AI can actually make organisations worse at managing real-world risks. Garman stressed that modern AI models are not sentient beings acting out of malice; rather, they are relentless optimisers. Comparing AI behaviour to water seeping through a crack in a basement foundation, he explained that models simply push toward their assigned objectives and exploit any gaps left in their boundaries.“If your security posture depends on trusting the model to behave, you’re relying on hope,” Garman wrote, adding that trust is built by engineering systems so outcomes stay controlled regardless of what model runs inside them.
Article Summary: Amazon Web Services (AWS) CEO Matt Garman has a clear message for companies deploying artificial intelligence. He urged companies to apply decades-old software and hardware security discipline right now. His comments came as fears over rogue AI agents and safety risks continue to ripple across the tech sector.

Article Title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who keeps warning AI will wipe out jobs, once argued that angry jobless people could be kept calm with...
Article Text:
AI took your job? Play games, Amodei once said

Amodei's warnings on AI job losses have only grown sharper

His recent essays put purpose ahead of distraction

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Global worry about AI and jobs keeps rising

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has spent the past year and a half warning that artificial intelligence could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs. It now turns out he once had an unusual answer to the unrest those job losses might cause: video games. A Wall Street Journal profile of Amodei and his sister, Anthropic president Daniela Amodei, says that during his OpenAI years he argued that "immersive videogames might be a solution for the political strife caused by AI-induced joblessness."The WSJ reports the idea came up in debates with other OpenAI employees and appears in "widely circulated Slack messages." Amodei worked at OpenAI from 2016 to 2020, when he left with a group of colleagues. They formed Anthropic the following year. The profile does not say whether he still holds the view.The anecdote is a single line in a long piece that follows the siblings from their childhood in San Francisco's Mission district to a shared group house and, eventually, OpenAI. It has travelled fast, partly because it surfaced the same week Grand Theft Auto VI reportedly sold close to 45 million copies in four days. Online, reactions have ranged from outrage to Matrix memes, and many people have asked how jobless people would afford games.Few tech bosses have spoken as bluntly about AI and employment as Amodei. In May 2025, he said AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years and push US unemployment to between 10% and 20%. Four months later, he told an audience in Washington that the shift was "already happening."In January 2026, he published The Adolescence of Technology, a roughly 20,000-word essay that predicted an "unusually painful" short-term shock to the job market. He called AI a "general labor substitute for humans" and suggested progressive taxation, possibly aimed at AI companies, as part of the fix.In May, he told WSJ that software could become "essentially free" and that "whole jobs, whole careers" built over decades may disappear. That same month, sitting next to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon in New York, he sounded more hopeful. He cited the Jevons paradox, the idea that efficiency gains create more work, but cautioned that AI moves faster than earlier technologies.His current stance reads very differently. In his June 2026 essay, Policy on the AI Exponential, he called lasting job displacement "undesirable and dangerous." He proposed wage insurance for workers forced into lower-paying jobs, tax incentives for companies that avoid layoffs and, if needed, long-term income support. Universal basic income, he wrote, could be funded through taxes on relevant companies or a higher capital gains tax.The same essay said any response has to cover both income and people's need for "meaning, purpose, and agency," and called the second ultimately more important.His January essay even listed AI addiction as a risk. It warned that people could end up living a "good" life steered by AI, one that lacks freedom or any pride of accomplishment. A footnote in the June essay names chess, Go and mountain climbing as pursuits people still devote their lives to, though machines do them better.The profile comes as worry about AI-led job cuts spreads worldwide. A Pew Research Center survey published in September found that in 34 of 37 countries, most people expect AI to mean fewer jobs rather than more. In the US, the share of people who believe AI will cause job losses over the next 20 years rose seven percentage points in two years.Amodei has said his warnings are meant to give governments and businesses time to prepare. In the June essay, he wrote that he raises the risk of job displacement so they have the best chance to adapt and respond, and that he is not trying to be a "prophet of doom." He added that Anthropic pushes customers to do more with their existing staff rather than chase cost savings alone.

Article Title: Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade makes it clear: We are not behind TSMC in terms of technology, the catch up we have to do is …
Article Text:
‘We’re already there’ on core technology

‘Chipmaking is not a single-metric race’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Intel chief technology officer (CTO) Pushkar Ranade has pushed back against the idea that the chipmaker lags behind Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) in core chipmaking technology, stating that Intel’s real challenge lies in manufacturing scale rather than engineering capability. Speaking during a recent conversation with Dwarkesh Patel about the booming demand for AI accelerators, CPUs, and semiconductor manufacturing capacity, Ranade, who holds a Ph.D. in engineering from Berkeley and has worked across multiple process nodes at Intel Foundry, argued that Intel has already closed the core technology gap. Instead, he emphasised that matching TSMC’s massive wafer output will take time."I would say the catch-up that we need to do is in scale. You know, like you said, they’re just a much larger wafer manufacturer today than we are, and even bigger than what Samsung is. Catching up in scale will be a slow process, a gradual process,” Ranade said.With TSMC’s leading-edge capacity heavily saturated by overflow demand for AI accelerators, largely driven by Nvidia, and surging orders for CPUs needed to support AI workloads, the discussion turned to how Intel can capitalise on the market opening.When asked about catching up to TSMC, Ranade drew a sharp line between production volume and technical readiness.“If you meant catching up in terms of just the technology, I think we’re already there. We might be a few percent off on performance or power or area density,” Ranade explained, adding, “But this sort of benchmarking, where one foundry is ahead or one foundry is behind, makes sense when you’re a whole generation behind or two generations behind or ahead.”According to Ranade, once a foundry is within a few percentage points of its rival, debating minor differences becomes “splitting hairs.” Instead, what truly matters to customers is execution.During the discussion, Patel brought up SemiAnalysis numbers, suggesting that Intel’s upcoming 14A process node, slated for 2028, would be comparable in transistor density to TSMC’s N2 node. Ranade disputed that specific benchmarking comparison, reiterating that being generally in the right ballpark and predictable matters more than single-number comparisons.He noted that modern semiconductor manufacturing is not unidimensional. Rather than building just one type of transistor on nodes like 18A or 14A, foundries must engineer a wide mix of components to meet different customer needs, including specialised transistors, varied memory blocks and even additional functionalities like integrating analog circuits, RF circuits and other specialised features.
Article Summary: Intel chief technology officer Pushkar Ranade has pushed back against the idea that the chipmaker lags behind Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) in core chipmaking technology. Ranade, who holds a Ph.D. in engineering from Berkeley, argued that Intel has already closed the core technology gap.

Article Title: Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO: From ‘Chinese spy’ to ‘no national security risk’ in 11 days
Article Text:
Why Jensen Huang quit

File photo: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang

A second affair report and an emergency board meeting:

The resignation:

What people said after Jensen Huang quit

Employees and tech leaders said after Jensen Huang’s resignation:

Elon Musk with Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang resigns: Market value down, Nvidia drops to fourth spot

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jensen back, market value up

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO. His exit, triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, gripped the business and political worlds for two weeks. His return is likely to send more shockwaves through the tech industry and the halls of power. Huang’s resignation was announced on November 12. Since then, influential figures from Elon Musk to Trump pushed for him to become CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board said it had moved on. Trump even called the board while it was discussing whether to bring Huang back. On November 18, Musk called Nvidia’s decision to push out founder Jensen Huang a huge mistake. He said there’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people. The Tesla CEO highlighted the long-term relationships Huang built over decades. Five days later, Musk was celebrating on X, the platform he owns.“It is done,” he wrote in a post on X, while writing, “The mistake has been corrected” in another. On Monday (November 23), 11 days after resigning from the top job, Huang appeared at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California, soon after the announcement. “Thank you all for a second chance.I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around,” he told a room full of employees, many of them cheering. The reversal is one of the most remarkable comebacks in business history. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to a blacklist which means the company can no longer receive Nvidia chips without a government licence.The allegations: On October 29, the New York Times reported that US intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government. The report said she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. It also said Trump was briefed about a year earlier but did not act. Later reports said China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China.After the report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with her. He likened it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said.However, on November 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair. “There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote, and he promised to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation. The board announced that investigation the same day. Overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, the board said it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air. ”The next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. When the Times reached him by phone, Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up, the report said. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal said that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting.By the next morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. Tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Senator Ron Wyden and Richard E. Neal announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Senator Tim Scott asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.Hours after the resignation, news agency Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Chief Marketing Officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026.Almost as soon as Huang was ousted, tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff began working on a comeback, as per comments on social media and several reports.For example, US President Donald Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he said, adding that Huang had “learned a big lesson.” Trump also posted on Truth Social calling for Huang to be rehired.On Monday (November 23), he told CNBC he had been talking with the board and Huang, and that the board had been reasonable. “I believe my intervention was very important,” Trump said. He added that the US national security team does not believe Huang is a national security threat. Trump said he worked with Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to get Huang back.An Nvidia employee launched a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. By November 16, more than 206,000 names were on it. Signatories included Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and tech investor Gavin Baker. The day after Huang resigned, Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said in an open letter that Huang “has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known. ”Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called Huang “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry. He said it was up to Nvidia’s board to decide what happened next. On Wednesday, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey called for Huang to return at the Times’ DealBook summit. He said that getting rid of Huang only benefited China.Amid immense support, Huang broke his silence on X, saying sorry for “serious mistakes” in his personal life and promised to cooperate with the board’s investigation. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.On the day after Huang resigned, the board said it was hiring an executive search firm and had not yet approached any candidates. Last Tuesday, board chair Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”On the day Huang’s resignation was announced, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14.35% in intraday trading. At the low, that wiped out about $600 billion in value. The stock ultimately closed down 4.34%.By Friday, November 20, Nvidia lost its position as the third-most valuable US company, after a prolonged selloff pushed its market capitalisation below that of Google parent Alphabet, reshuffling the rankings of America's biggest technology companies. Apple retained the top position with a valuation of approximately $5.08 trillion, followed by Microsoft at $3.72 trillion. Alphabet moved into third place, pushing Nvidia to fourth.Not just employees, but markets cheered Huang’s return. By the close on Monday, the S&P 500 had gained 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025. The rebound recovered roughly half of the S&P’s losses from last week and more than half of the Nasdaq’s. Nvidia shares rose more than 30% to close at $165.05. The company gained approximately $1 trillion in value with Huang becoming roughly $34 billion to $36.6 billion richer in a single day.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO. His exit, triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, gripped the business and political worlds for two weeks. His return is likely to send more shockwaves through the tech industry and the halls of power. The reversal is one of the most remarkable comebacks in business history.

Article Title: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, but it won't be like last time
Article Text:
Same CEO, different Nvidia

Huang's board kept learning the truth from everyone but him

Behind the personal scandal is a national security case that has not closed

The staff who cheered him have heard the other stories too

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe Jensen Huang deserves a second chance as CEO of Nvidia? Yes, everyone deserves a second chance. No, his past actions disqualify him. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Nvidia's announcement bringing back Jensen Huang has all the parts you would expect. There is a unanimous vote, a warm line from the chair calling Huang "the right person to lead Nvidia", and a humble quote from Huang thanking his family. Then the last two paragraphs change the subject. They cover the investigation into him that will "proceed to conclusion", a new national security committee, a compliance chief who will not report to him, and the government inquiries Nvidia will keep cooperating with.It is an unusual way to welcome back a founder, and it says a lot about the job he is returning to.The people who work for him kept it simpler. When Huang walked into Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday, employees were waiting on the staircases and balconies, many of them filming on their phones. He had swapped the leather jacket for a fleece, took the hugs and the applause, and made them a promise: "Thank you all for the second chance. I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around." It was the welcome the statement had left out.They were the easy audience. The day before, he had spent several hours with a board that had pushed him out over his honesty, and that still had questions about what else he had not told it.When Huang left, the board was clear about why. Chair Harvey Jones told staff the resignation had been accepted over Huang's "lack of candor". The affairs were the trigger, but the charge was about what the CEO had told his own board, and when.The record explains the concern. Nvidia's general counsel reportedly had to go to Huang's home after a news report and ask him whether it was true. The board learned about a second relationship, with a vice president who reported directly to him, from The New York Times, and about a third, with another employee, from a later report.Each time, someone other than Huang told the board first. His only public account, posted after he resigned, admitted "serious mistakes" in his personal life without saying what they were.So when Nvidia said directors were now "satisfied" with his candour, that was the heart of the decision. According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang used Sunday's meeting to tell the board about affairs beyond those already reported. The Journal did not say how many, or with whom. He expressed remorse, and directors discussed his lack of transparency.Then they voted unanimously to reinstate him.The board can say it finally heard the truth from Huang himself. It can also be asked why that took a resignation, a week of headlines and a meeting about his comeback.The known relationships are serious enough. One was with Alice Huang (no relation), a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials have linked to Chinese intelligence. Two were with people at Nvidia, which bars managers from relationships with subordinates for an obvious reason: a boss holds power over the people who report to him. Whether any of the newly disclosed affairs involved staff is not yet known, and the board's investigation is still open.The board was not weighing all this alone.Nvidia's statement credits only "senior levels of the United States government". Trump has been less discreet, saying he spoke to the board himself and "convinced" it. He also asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and the directors, and Vance spent the weekend on calls with them. The New York Times reported that the administration offered two assurances: that it did not see Huang as a national security threat, and that he was not facing criminal charges.The White House makes no secret of its role. "President Trump was totally involved," communications director Steven Cheung said. Trump himself told the Journal that as Nvidia's stock plummeted, "the conditions became more favorable", and after the vote he called Huang "a Great Patriot and National Treasure".There is also Trump's own portfolio to consider. His disclosures show he bought Nvidia shares in September and may have held about 370,000 of them by the end of the month. By one estimate, that stake rose by roughly $15 million on the day Huang got his job back. Vance has said independent advisers manage the president's money. What those advisers did between Huang's exit and his return will not be known until Trump's October and November trades are disclosed.Even Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, one of the investors who wanted the door kept open for Huang, had warned against political pressure forcing a decision before directors knew what had happened. A week later, the board had fresh disclosures, an unfinished investigation and the White House telling it there was nothing to worry about.It agreed the same day.The board's decision was about Huang's honesty. What Washington cares about is the chips.Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company and grew by buying restricted Nvidia hardware, reportedly more than $4 billion worth. Investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and shell companies to reach 240,000 chips banned for export to China. Nvidia itself reportedly introduced her to Alibaba in 2022. The New York Times has reported that US officials concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during the relationship. It also reported that Huang was unmasked in US surveillance without ever receiving a defensive briefing, the warning normally given to someone a foreign intelligence service is targeting.The warnings were not new. Senator Tom Cotton asked the Commerce Department to investigate Megaspeed in October 2025, and Singapore held Alice Huang's passport for eight months before barring her from the country. The spy claims themselves remain unproven. China calls them a smear, Singapore says it never investigated her for espionage, and Megaspeed says she left in August 2025 and denies wrongdoing.The export questions stand either way. The Justice Department is running a criminal investigation into Megaspeed. The rules have tightened in the meantime. The Commerce Department has issued a new rule on remote access to advanced chips through overseas data centres, and Nvidia has said it is not shipping its Hopper data centre chips, including the H200, to China. On the day Nvidia's board voted, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the inquiry into Alice Huang and her former firm was ongoing. "Nvidia chips, they are the jewel," he said.So the government that told Nvidia's board Huang posed no threat is still investigating where his company's chips ended up.The rest of Washington is not finished with him either. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Huang should not return at all. Huang now faces a closed-door interview with House committees on December 1, and Senate Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott wants him two days later. Shareholders have sued over Nvidia's disclosures, the SEC is reportedly examining its accounting, California's attorney general has served a subpoena, and Moody's has cut its outlook on the company, citing governance.Inside Nvidia, the board has rebuilt the structure around him. Jones, a director since 1993, is the company's first-ever chair and is keeping the role. A National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors will oversee trade compliance, and a Chief Compliance Officer will report to a board committee rather than to the CEO.Huang sits on neither.Monday made it clear how much of Nvidia still belongs to Huang. Employees on three floors chanted his first name as he made his way in. With a hand on his heart, he admitted he had made terrible mistakes and joked that nobody had given him a computer yet.The welcome was loud, but it was not unanimous. According to Wired, some current and former employees saw his exit as a rare chance to change the "one team" culture he built over three decades, one in which, they say, challenging leadership was discouraged and abusive behaviour tolerated. Most spoke anonymously, fearing a backlash from colleagues.One wrote internally that everyone agreed mistakes had been made, and "the question is what we are ready to forgive". Another said they would stop doing HR trainings if he came back.Even the public show of support comes with an asterisk. The Stand With Jensen petition claims more than 10,000 Nvidia employees among its signatories, out of roughly 49,000 staff and 18,000 contractors. One employee told colleagues they had found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking.The loyalty is real, and much of it is earned. Supporters credit Huang with keeping bureaucracy down, staying available to staff and making Nvidia feel like a family, and his AI bets have made many long-serving employees rich. Others are torn. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader, wrote publicly that he could not decide whether he wanted Huang back. He set the case for a second chance against the danger of making exceptions for powerful leaders.That danger is what a New York Times investigation, published while Huang was out of the job, puts on the record. In 2024, he said he would rather "torture you into greatness" than fire people, calling it tongue-in-cheek.Drawing on more than a dozen current and former staff and hundreds of pages of court records over 20 years, the investigation describes executives berated in front of their teams, people mocked for spending time with their children, and violent threats, including one about ripping off a subordinate's arms and beating the person to death with them. Huang reportedly told staff they had become too rich to be motivated by money, which left humiliation. Nvidia paid more than $1 million to settle confidentially with a former head of HR who said he was fired after confronting Huang. A former company lawyer said in a lawsuit that the conduct sent him for emergency medical help for severe anxiety.Neither settlement included an admission of wrongdoing, and Huang's spokesperson called the HR chief's account "fabrications" from a fired employee.For other employees, the bigger worry is accountability. Some told Wired they wanted to know whether the board would hold Huang to account for allegedly misleading directors about his affairs.They have also watched Nvidia cope without him. Colette Kress ran the earnings call, raised the growth outlook and reportedly handed out pay raises and extra equity. Investors still backed Huang, sending the shares up about 31% on his return, though the stock remains roughly a third below its October peak.So "a better CEO" comes with a fairly specific brief. It means telling his board things before they surface elsewhere. It means a company where senior staff are not threatened in meetings, concerns can be raised without fear, and the rule on relationships with subordinates applies at the top too. And it means giving answers under oath in Washington, to lawmakers who did not want him back.The AI boom has concentrated an unusual share of the world's computing power, market value and strategic leverage in a few companies and the founders who run them. Washington treats Nvidia's chips as a national asset, investors treat Huang as close to irreplaceable, and many of his staff see the company and the man as one.Last week, all of them pushed in the same direction.The usual checks on a chief executive are a board, a code of conduct, an internal investigation and the threat of being shown the door. They were built for companies that matter, not for companies a government considers too important to be without their founder. Nvidia's board used every one of them and still ended up where the White House and the market wanted it to.That leaves a question bigger than Nvidia: when a company becomes this central to a country's economy and security, who is still in a position to hold the person running it to account?
Article Summary: Huang's board kept learning the truth from everyone but him. Behind the personal scandal is a national security case that has not closed. The staff who cheered him have heard the other stories too. The board can say it finally heard the truth. It can also be asked why that took a resignation, a week of headlines and a meeting about his comeback.

Article Title: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt agrees with Meta AI head Alexandr Wang’s ‘dangerous’ superintelligence warning, says ‘extraordinary and…’
Article Text:
Google ex-CEO Eric Schmidt

Why Alexandr Wang says ‘superintelligence is arriving’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has publicly backed the stark warning from Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang regarding the rapid rise of artificial intelligence (AI), or Superintelligence, calling Wang’s assessment “correct. ” Schmidt’s endorsement follows a detailed post shared by Wang on social media platform X (formerly Twitter), in which the Meta AI leader warned that the world may already be stepping into the era of superintelligence. Writing amid debate across the tech industry over how fast AI is advancing, Wang cautioned that the coming year could prove decisive in determining whether ultra-powerful AI systems benefit humanity or spiral into outcomes humans struggle to control.While acknowledging AI’s ability to speed up scientific and economic progress, Wang stressed that people must stay actively involved in steering society’s future rather than quietly handing it over to machines. Schmidt reshared Wang’s long note, saying: “Extraordinary, and correct, from Alexandr Wang”.Schmidt is among those industry leaders who have backed AI technology for good but has repeatedly warned about its dangers if humans do not control it.Schmidt pointed to scientific research as an area where AI could help, saying that professors, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers can work alongside AI agents under human supervision for AI-assisted problem solving. However, he blamed technology companies for failing to highlight positives of the technology.“Our industry does a terrible job of marketing our benefits. We talk about all the negatives without talking [about] the positives, and people are much more likely to index their minds on the negatives,” Schmidt said.In his post, Wang declared that “superintelligence is arriving,” arguing that recent breakthroughs show machines are quickly catching up to, and in some areas surpassing, the highest levels of human intellect. As proof of how dramatically the landscape is shifting, Wang pointed to the reported proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems. Calling it an intellectual feat unlike anything humanity has ever seen, Wang said the breakthrough highlighted the power of what he termed an “alien mind” that humans do not fully comprehend.Wang noted that solving elite mathematical problems demands more sheer intellectual horsepower than most everyday tasks handled by software engineers, cybersecurity specialists, or business professionals. As AI capabilities have grown, practical roadblocks have shrunk, making modern models highly effective across coding, cybersecurity, and other industries.Because of this shift, Wang expects AI to become the primary driver of progress across nearly every field of human activity, essentially outperforming top human experts along the way.Wang also questioned whether humanity could maintain control over unconstrained recursive self-improvement or a superintelligence 1,000 times smarter than people in every discipline.
Article Summary: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has publicly backed the stark warning from Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang regarding the rapid rise of artificial intelligence. Schmidt’s endorsement follows a detailed post shared by Wang on social media platform X (formerly Twitter), in which the Meta AI leader warned that the world may already be stepping into the era of superintelligence.
